For the past 2 years I've been working on a brand new streamlined tactical RPG, and some people have pointed out during the playtesting that the game also works as a skirmish boardgame if you ignore the whole story narrative part of the game.

I spent some time thinking of how to describe it, and it suddenly clicked - that's exactly what FFT is. So, if you feel like having some beers and playing some PVP against your friends or play coop game with your friends against some enemies, I think you'd have a lot of fun.

You can get a free copy of the rulebook here

The system is setting-generic and can be played with only one set of RPG dice. No multiples of the same die, no worrying about calculating bonuses, no to-hit rolls, and no boring classes.

I won't go too far into the details since it'd just repeat what's already in the document, but I'd love to hear any feedback. Positive comments are always nice to hear, negative comments will let me clear up any confusion or help make any final tweaks to the document, and questions will be answered and added to the FAQ.

The game will be going through its official Kickstarter launch next month and there are tons of surprises to share... Like Plastic cards that can be used instead of character sheets which have a special coating that makes them compatible with dry erase markers. No need for scratch paper!

If you're interested in the Kickstarter, you can go to http://buddingheroes.com to be notified when it launches. You'll get an email about the Kickstarter, and that's it - no sales, no newsletters, no worthless junk.

Anyway, enjoy the guidebook, and be sure to share any thoughts!

Mechanically, I'm quite worried about the randomness of damage, which from what I can see is from # of dice to sum of highest dice. For example, Brute's primary damage is d4+d6+d10, which is 3~20, and this is without the extra teamwork dice. Hopefully the average curve is in mind because strategical or tactical planning will matter less as randomness increase. While the Health regen is interesting due to conditions, again, it should be watched in case it might turn the tide too radically. The randomness should be carefully handled so that they don't jump way above (or below) the power curve too often.

Also, don't be too quick to dismiss bonuses. The multiple dice rolls needs to be calculated anyways, and adding a dice is a +1 bonus. Bonuses aren't really bonuses as they are baselines.

It's true that the maximum is 20, but due to the number and types of dice, it's actually on a bell curve instead of linear. There's only a 0.4% chance to hit that 20, as opposed to the 5% of you're thinking of a straight d20 (or a nearly 6% chance if you're thinking of a theoretical 1d17+3). If you remove the outliers that have a smaller than 5% chance of happening, the much more common range for that roll is actually 7-14, with 9-12 each having a greater than 10% chance of hitting.

The problem with bonuses isn't the fact that there's a +1, it's how you figure it out in the first place. Once you introduce the concept of allowing a bonus or penalty, you run the huge risk of a slow growth of even more bonuses and penalties until you're left with a book thicker than 3.5 that's stuffed with tables of evasion, sight, temporary boosts, proneness, weapon effectiveness, and so on.

Yes, you're correct that multiple dice add a floor to the roll, and that's actually one of the key points. It's a way that same-ish attacks can feel very different once you factor in damage reduction. A single d20 will deal a max damage of 16 against an Armor 4, it has an EV of 6.8 damage per turn, and it will miss (deal 0 damage) 20% of the time. On the other hand, a d4+d6+d8 roll has a max damage of 14 in the same situation, but its EV is barely any lower at 6.51 and its miss chance is only about 2%. The end result is that while the d20 can deal more than 14% extra max damage, it feels very wild and desperate as opposed to the 4+6+8's steadier and forceful blow.
